articles.title: Fluence Has a $6.4 Billion Backlog but Pushed $400 Million of Deliveries Out. Is the AI-Power Story Breaking?
articles.summary: In its August 5 results, Fluence Energy ended the fiscal third quarter with a $6.4 billion backlog, yet about $400 million of project deliveries moved into f...
articles.body:
In its August 5 results, Fluence Energy ended the fiscal third quarter with a $6.4 billion backlog, yet about $400 million of project deliveries moved into fiscal 2027. The tension between demand and execution sits at the heart of the stock. Fluence Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ: FLNC ) has become an AI-power proxy because batteries can help data centers secure capacity and stabilize grids. Its latest numbers show how a large revenue opportunity can still produce disappointing shareholder economics.

Battery energy storage solutions. Photo from Fluence Energy website

There is substance behind the optimistic view. Fiscal third-quarter revenue increased 7.9% to $649.8 million, order intake exceeded $1.44 billion, and backlog reached $6.4 billion. Fluence said its data-center business totaled about $850 million, including $550 million of awards tied to a hyperscaler. That pipeline places battery storage inside identifiable AI infrastructure projects rather than leaving it as a broad grid theme.

Execution is the problem. Gross margin fell to 5.1% from 14.8% a year earlier, and net loss widened to $44.3 million. Management said about $400 million of project deliveries shifted into fiscal 2027. It reduced the midpoint of full-year revenue guidance from $3.4 billion to $3.0 billion and moved the adjusted EBITDA midpoint from positive $50 million to negative $10 million. A large backlog offers limited comfort if timing slips and project economics deteriorate.

Professional investors became more numerous before the quarterly report. Insider Monkey counted 39 hedge funds holding Fluence Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:FLNC) at the end of Q2, up from 31 in Q1. Point72 Asset Management reported 1,301,799 shares as of June 30, while D. E. Shaw reported 3,194,735. Those positions offer a snapshot of long exposure; they do not identify either manager's present view or complete portfolio.

Reported short interest was substantial. The August 14 settlement showed 25.45 million shares short, up 13.9% from 22.35 million on July 31, with 2.7 days to cover. Published float estimates diverge sharply, making the raw position and its change more dependable than a percentage. The positioning creates squeeze potential while raising the burden of proof.

The AI-power story remains under pressure because Fluence has yet to convert demand into reliable margins and delivery timing. Management now needs to show that delayed projects remain profitable and the data-center business turns into cash. Investors should track gross margin by project mix, working-capital use, and the portion of backlog that converts each quarter. Those measures will separate a temporary schedule problem from contracts that were priced too aggressively.

articles.title: RingCentral Says Paid-AI Customers Now Represent 13% of ARR as Revenue Grew 6%. Has the Market Already Priced It In?
articles.summary: On July 23, RingCentral said customers using at least one paid native AI product represented about 13% of annual recurring revenue, and that measure had doub...
articles.body:
On July 23, RingCentral said customers using at least one paid native AI product represented about 13% of annual recurring revenue, and that measure had doubled year over year. That gives its AI strategy a measurable commercial foothold. By September 2, RingCentral, Inc. (NYSE: RNG ) had already gained about 141% over the preceding year and traded near a four-year high, leaving investors to decide whether a revived business can keep compounding.

Second-quarter results give the bulls evidence. Revenue rose 5.9% to $657 million, subscription revenue increased 5.8% to $634 million, and GAAP operating margin reached 7.7%. Customers using paid native AI products represented 13% of annual recurring revenue, double the year-earlier level. That measure describes the ARR attached to customers using a paid AI product; it is neither standalone AI revenue nor proof that AI caused every dollar in the cohort. The distinction matters when investors price AI-driven expansion. Management also raised its full-year revenue range, lifted free-cash-flow guidance to $615 million to $625 million, and increased the dividend 67%.

The challenge is that headline growth remains modest. AI adoption can deepen customer spending, but communications software is competitive and switching costs are not absolute. Microsoft, Zoom, contact-center specialists, and newer AI-native services can pressure pricing. The stock's large rebound also means improving profitability is no longer a secret, and the margin of safety has narrowed with the rerating.

Hedge funds became slightly more numerous during Q2. Insider Monkey counted 27 funds holding RingCentral, Inc. (NYSE:RNG), up from 25 in Q1. AQR Capital Management reported 1,537,795 shares as of June 30. That snapshot records historical positioning rather than proving how the fund views the stock today.

Short interest was meaningful but declining. The August 14 settlement showed 7.06 million shares short, or 9.12% of float, down 7.7% from 7.65 million on July 31, with 3.8 days to cover. The decline does not reveal why individual traders changed exposure.

RingCentral's AI story is becoming measurable because the ARR share tied to customers using at least one paid product, rather than demo activity, has doubled. The remaining question is whether AI can lift total company growth beyond the mid-single digits while margins expand. Net retention, the ARR share tied to customers using paid AI products, seat growth, and free cash flow should move together if the strategy is working. A higher AI-usage percentage alone could otherwise reflect adoption inside a business whose overall revenue pool is expanding too slowly to reward long-term shareholders adequately in today's market.

articles.title: WhiteFiber’s Cloud and Colocation Revenue Grew With 6 Million Shares Sold Short. Is This AI Data-Center Bet a Squeeze or a Trap?
articles.summary: WhiteFiber’s August 12 filing showed that second-quarter colocation and cloud-services revenue both increased, while 6.04 million shares were sold short at t...
articles.body:
WhiteFiber's August 12 filing showed that second-quarter colocation and cloud-services revenue both increased, while 6.04 million shares were sold short at the August 14 settlement. That pairing captures the market's argument over an ambitious AI-infrastructure buildout. WhiteFiber, Inc. (NASDAQ: WYFI ) describes itself as a vertically integrated provider of AI-optimized data centers and GPU cloud services. The model offers exposure to both the buildings and the computing capacity inside them, but it also requires unusually heavy capital and precise execution.

The attraction is easy to see. Dense AI clusters need power, cooling, networking, and specialized operations. WhiteFiber can earn colocation revenue while also selling compute through its cloud platform. Second-quarter colocation revenue rose to $4.7 million from $1.7 million, while cloud-services revenue climbed to $23.8 million from $16.6 million, although the quarter included a $12.3 million customer-termination fee that substantially offset lost recurring GPU-service revenue from that customer. If capacity fills and customers sign longer contracts, fixed infrastructure can produce meaningful operating leverage.

The capital structure keeps the story speculative. At June 30, WhiteFiber had $56.1 million of cash, $83.2 million of debt, $222.6 million carrying value of convertible notes, and a $28.6 million working-capital deficit. On August 21, it closed $310 million of new 5% convertible notes due 2032 and received about $298.5 million net. It used $118.5 million of the proceeds plus 6.3 million shares to exchange $198.15 million principal of its older notes. The refinancing improved liquidity, but it also added interest expense and potential dilution.

Professional investors were moving in opposite directions. Insider Monkey's database showed 16 hedge funds holding WhiteFiber, Inc. (NASDAQ:WYFI) at the end of Q2, down from 17 in Q1. Citadel Advisors reported 1,174,300 shares as of June 30.

Short positioning is a defining technical feature. The August 14 settlement showed 6.04 million shares short, down 6.5% from 6.47 million on July 31, with 4.1 days to cover. Good contract or utilization news could force covering; disappointing execution would strengthen the fundamental bear case.

WhiteFiber is both a squeeze candidate and a fundamental test. Scarce AI-ready infrastructure creates upside, while leverage and losses give bearish investors a case. Investors should focus on contracted power, utilization, recurring revenue, debt terms, and cash conversion. Execution now matters more than ambition. The August refinancing provides capital to build, but a commercially attractive data center can still produce poor equity returns when interest costs or dilution absorb the upside.

articles.title: Monolithic Power Revenue Jumped 48%. Can AI Power Chips Keep the Momentum Going?
articles.summary: On July 30, Monolithic Power Systems reported second-quarter revenue of $980.6 million, up 47.6% from a year earlier and 21.9% sequentially. The pace puts it...
articles.body:
On July 30, Monolithic Power Systems reported second-quarter revenue of $980.6 million, up 47.6% from a year earlier and 21.9% sequentially. The pace puts its AI opportunity into reported results. Monolithic Power Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ: MPWR ) does not sell AI accelerators. It supplies the power-management components that help those expensive processors operate efficiently, making the company a picks-and-shovels bet on rising compute density.

Close-up of Silicon Die are being Extracted from Semiconductor Wafer and Attached to Substrate by Pick and Place Machine. Computer Chip Manufacturing at Fab. Semiconductor Packaging Process.

That position creates a clear advantage. More powerful accelerators require increasingly sophisticated voltage regulation and power delivery, creating opportunities for higher content per system. Monolithic Power's broad product portfolio and engineering relationships can make designs sticky once qualified. Q2 gross margin of 55.2% indicates that recent growth preserved the basic economics of the business. Investors should still separate data-center momentum from companywide demand, because a strong AI category can coexist with softer orders across automotive, industrial, storage, and consumer applications. That distinction matters most if ordering momentum begins to slow.

The risks sit in expectations and concentration. Semiconductor demand is cyclical, customers can redesign systems, and large buyers have leverage over pricing. AI infrastructure orders may be strong while consumer, automotive, or industrial markets weaken. After a powerful rerating, the stock needs more than rapid revenue growth to justify elevated expectations. It needs confidence that those gains can persist without inventory corrections or competitive losses.

Hedge-fund ownership expanded sharply during Q2. Insider Monkey tracked 69 funds holding Monolithic Power Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:MPWR) at quarter-end, up from 49 in Q1. Adage Capital Management reported 96,352 shares as of June 30. Citadel also disclosed puts covering 85,300 shares, a reminder that 13F long and option positions can serve different purposes within a broader strategy.

Short interest is comparatively moderate. The August 14 settlement showed 1.84 million shares short, or 3.88% of float, down 13.4% from July 31, with 2.7 days to cover. Forced covering is unlikely to be the main engine of the investment case. Pricing alone cannot protect a richly valued cyclical supplier from weaker demand.

Monolithic Power is turning AI power complexity into reported revenue. Q2 supports that thesis, while the valuation leaves little room for an ordinary semiconductor pause. Investors should watch design wins, customer diversity, and gross margin. Another quarter of strong enterprise-data revenue, without margin deterioration or an offsetting correction elsewhere, would provide the cleanest confirmation. That combination would show the company is gaining valuable content rather than benefiting from a temporary surge in customer ordering.

articles.title: Nvidia Says Memory Pricing Has Turned ‘Extreme’ and Is ‘Headed Even Higher Into Next Year,’ But Its Own Price Increases Are Already Executed
articles.summary: CFO Colette Kress noted "extreme pricing conditions in memory" on the Q2 earnings call.
articles.body:
Nvidia (NVDA) CFO Colette Kress told investors last week that the company is seeing "extreme pricing conditions in memory," that the increases have "exceeded our prior expectations," and that they are "headed even higher into next year." Colette Kress said this in prepared remarks on Nvidia's fiscal second-quarter earnings call on Aug. 26, and then delivered the line companies almost never say plainly: "As a result, we are resetting expectations today."

Memory is not an exotic part. It is the DRAM in a phone, the RAM in a laptop, the storage in a game console, and one of the most expensive ingredients in a graphics card… and three companies make nearly all of it. Kress was describing the market for AI server memory, not the shelf price of a laptop, and Nvidia said nothing at all about consumer devices. But those products draw on the same suppliers and the same fabs, which is why a chip company's margin guidance is worth reading even if you never buy a chip.

The guidance is where the admission gets specific. Gross margin was 75% in the quarter that was just reported. Kress guided to 74% in the current quarter and told analysts that Nvidia expects "margins to bottom in Q4 in the 71% to 72% range before settling at 72% to 73% in [fiscal 2028] as executed price increases take effect in Q1." Executed, not contemplated. Nvidia is absorbing part of the memory bill and passing part of it forward, and it has already decided how much.

Sponsored Content: Invest in the Platform Giving Everyday Investors Access to Private Markets

The company also volunteered the cause, which is the unusual part. "Memory scarcity today is being driven in large part by the AI buildout itself," Kress said, and "unlike a component that simply raises our cost with no offset benefit, tighter memory supply is a symptom of the same demand surge that's driving our own growth." Nvidia is not presenting itself as a bystander to the shortage.

It is also the largest single buyer inside it. Nvidia's supplier purchase commitments stood at roughly $279 billion in its most recent quarterly filing — capacity reserved years ahead of when the parts are needed. Tom's Hardware reports that about $160 billion of that relates to memory specifically. That split is not obviously a disclosed line item in the filing, and it should be read as that outlet's reporting rather than as a company figure.

articles.title: TCS HyperVault to invest Rs 70,000 crore in AI data centre in Hyderabad
articles.summary: TCS HyperVault to invest ₹70,000 crore in a 1GW AI data centre campus on 264 acres in Hyderabad, creating 7,000 jobs and supporting AI workloads.
articles.body: HYDERABAD: One of India’s largest artificial intelligence data centre campuses is all set to come up in Hyderabad with TCS HyperVault, a subsidiary of Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), announcing plans to invest Rs 70,000 crore for a gigawatt-scale facility in Hyderabad.It will cater to frontier AI companies like OpenAI, hyperscalers and global enterprises.TCS has been allocated 264 acres for the project at Bharat Future City that is expected to create about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs across technical, construction, engineering and operations roles.The project is expected to become functional within 18 to 24 months.HyperVault CEO and managing director Deepesh Kiran Nanda said the campus would be designed for high rack-density compute, liquid cooling, large power blocks and next-generation GPU systems.He said the facility would support future advances in AI hardware.“This will be the first time that India will witness high rack density compute of more than 170 kW. The data centre will be on a par or even ahead of anything that has been built globally,” he said.The campus, to be developed in phases based on customer demand and evolving technology requirements, is expected to incorporate green energy and water-neutral design principles.It is being designed for high-density GPU deployments and will support AI training, inference and advanced computing workloads, TCS said.Telangana competing with China, Germany & Japan, says CMThe investment was announced after a high-level TCS delegation led by its CEO & managing director K Krithivasan met Telangana chief minister A Revanth Reddy at the secretariat on Saturday afternoon and exchanged MoUs.The announcement comes months after the chief minister met Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran at Davos.“Future City is reality. My dream is coming true,” said the CM, urging the TCS team to target inauguration of the project by Telangana Formation Day on June 2, 2028.He said TCS already employed more than 83,000 people in Hyderabad and urged the company to take this number beyond one lakh.Revanth said the state had maintained policy continuity for nearly three decades despite changes in govts. He said Telangana is not competing with neighbouring states but with economies such as China, Germany, Japan, South Korea and Singapore.The CM also linked the project to Telangana’s long-term economic goals, saying the state aimed to become a $1 trillion economy by 2034 and a $3 trillion economy by 2047.He said AI infrastructure would be critical to that ambition, while the project would also generate secure blue-collar employment in areas such as electrical work, plumbing, water systems and data centre operations.IT and industries minister D Sridhar Babu said the project showed Telangana’s ability to move quickly on major investments.“Telangana means business. We move at speed and with clarity of process that matches the expectations of the tech and corporate world,” he said. He said the project would make Hyderabad a world-scale AI infrastructure hub.Krithivasan said HyperVault was part of TCS’ “infrastructure-to-intelligence” strategy and that Hyderabad’s scale, talent base and govt support made it the natural choice for the investment that will be made by TCS along with its partners.OpenAI’s compute CTO Uday Rudraraju, who joined virtually, said the scale and ambition of the project were significant and reflected India’s growing role in foundational AI infrastructure.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Hyderabad | Silver Rate in Hyderabad | Bank Holidays in Hyderabad | Public Holidays in Hyderabad | Hyderabad AQI | Weather in Hyderabad | Petrol Price in Hyderabad | Diesel Price in Hyderabad | CNG Price in Hyderabad | LPG Price in HyderabadStay updated with the latest Hyderabad news.
